opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly my heuristic has shifted a lot over the past year as the agents have gotten better.

The first thing I ask is: can I describe what "done" looks like in a couple of sentences? If I can write down a clear spec, like the inputs, the expected behavior, and ideally some way to check it, like a test that should pass or a command that should run cleanly, then it's a great candidate to hand off. The agent does really well when it has a tight feedback loop it can run on its own. Where it struggles is when the task is really "figure out what we should build," because then you end up going back and forth so much that you might as well have done it yourself.

The second thing is how separable it is from what I'm doing right now. If it touches the same files I'm actively editing, or it depends on a design decision I haven't made yet, spinning it off just creates merge pain and rework. But if it's a self-contained chunk, like adding an endpoint, writing tests for a module, fixing a bug with a clear repro, or doing a refactor with a well-defined pattern, those are perfect to fire off in parallel and come back to.

And then there's a cost-benefit piece around review. The real bottleneck isn't the agent writing the code anymore, it's me reading it. So I think about whether reviewing it will be much cheaper than writing it. For a lot of tasks, the kind of tedious but easy-to-verify stuff, it absolutely is. For something subtle, like concurrency or security-sensitive logic, the review burden can be just as high as writing it, so the win is smaller.

What I've noticed is that the bar keeps dropping. I used to only hand off really small, obvious things. Now my default is closer to "why not kick it off?" Starting a thread is cheap. If it comes back wrong, I've lost a few minutes, and often even a failed attempt teaches me something about the problem. So increasingly the question isn't "is this worth starting?" but "do I have enough clarity to give it a fair shot?"

r001.rationale: The response says a task should be separable from current work, noting that touching the same files being actively edited creates merge pain and that self-contained chunks are good candidates for parallel threads.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is: can I describe what "done" looks like well enough that I'd be comfortable not watching? That's really the test. If I can write down the task in a way where the agent can tell on its own whether it succeeded — there's a test that should pass, there's a spec, there's a reference implementation it's porting from — then it's a great candidate to spin off as its own thread. I kick it off, I go do something else, I come back and review.

Where it falls down is when the task is really a design question wearing a coding costume. If I don't actually know what I want yet, and I'm going to figure it out by looking at the code and reacting to it, then handing that off is kind of a trap. The agent will happily make a hundred decisions I didn't realize were decisions, and then I'm spending more time untangling its assumptions than I would have spent just sitting with it interactively.

So the second thing I look at is how much the task is going to touch. If it's well-scoped — a new module, a migration, a bug where I already know roughly where it lives — great, go. If it's going to cut across the whole codebase and interact with other things in flight, that's where you get merge pain and weird emergent breakage, and I'd rather be in the loop.

And then honestly the last factor is just: how expensive is it for me to verify the result? Some things are cheap to check — run the tests, skim the diff, done. Some things, like a subtle performance change or something security-adjacent, I'm going to have to read every line anyway. If reviewing it costs me as much as writing it, the independence doesn't buy me much. The sweet spot is tasks that are tedious to do but cheap to check. That's where you get the real leverage from running a bunch of these in parallel.

r001.rationale: The response says to consider how much the task touches and recommends staying involved when it cuts across the codebase or interacts with other work in flight, identifying separation from ongoing code as a criterion.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: can you give the agent enough context to make progress independently, and can you tell whether it succeeded? It doesn’t necessarily have to be a small task. A larger task with a clear objective and a good way to test the result can be a better candidate than a tiny task that depends on a lot of unstated assumptions.

There’s also an overhead tradeoff. You have to explain the task, let the agent work, and then review what it did. If doing it yourself would be faster than explaining and reviewing it, a separate thread probably isn’t worth it. But if you can hand off a reasonably self-contained piece of work and do something else while it runs, that’s where it becomes useful.

r001.rationale: The response says the task should be self-contained and workable independently, but does not identify separation from the code currently being written as a criterion.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: can you give the agent enough context to make progress independently, and can you tell whether it succeeded? If you can describe a reasonably self-contained task, point it at the relevant code, and give it a way to validate the result, that’s a good candidate for a separate thread.

The other consideration is how coupled it is to what you’re doing. If you’ll need to keep interrupting it because you’re changing the same code or making decisions that affect its approach, the coordination overhead can outweigh the benefit. But if you can hand it something, go work on something else, and come back to a result you can review, that’s where it becomes really useful.

r001.rationale: The response says to consider how coupled the task is to current work and warns that changing the same code can create coordination overhead, communicating code separation as a criterion for a separate thread.
